opus-5.5.text:
I think what I value most about New York is that it constantly pulls you out of your own bubble. In research, especially in AI, it's very easy to live entirely inside your work. You wake up, check experiments, read papers, talk to students, and the day is gone. If you're in a place where everyone does the same thing, that loop just keeps reinforcing itself.

New York doesn't really let you do that. Walk a few blocks and you run into a jazz club, a small gallery, a pottery studio, a climbing gym, some strange experimental theater thing in a basement. The density of people doing things that have nothing to do with machine learning is very high. That's healthy for me. It reminds me the world is much bigger than benchmarks and leaderboards.

The barrier to trying something new is also very low here. You don't have to plan a big trip or commit a lot. You can just walk into a class one evening, see if you like it, and if not, try something else next week. That kind of low-cost exploration is valuable, and honestly it's similar to how I think about research: you want an environment where you can try many small things, fail cheaply, and occasionally find something that really resonates.

There's also a quieter benefit. A lot of my best thinking happens when I'm not thinking about work directly, when I'm watching a performance or just wandering around the city. Your mind makes connections it wouldn't make at a desk. So hobbies aren't just a break from research for me. In a way they feed back into it, by keeping me curious and giving me different ways of seeing things.

r001.rationale: The response values New York’s low-barrier opportunities to try hobbies and describes benefits from engaging in them, but does not say that simply having those opportunities brings joy even without taking advantage of them.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: You know, one thing I really appreciate about New York is that the city almost forces you out of your bubble. As a researcher, it's very easy to live inside your work. You wake up thinking about an experiment, you go to the lab, you talk to students about the same problem, you come home and read papers. In a lot of places, that loop just closes on itself. In New York, it doesn't, because the moment you step outside, the city is full of people doing completely different things, and they're doing them with total seriousness.

So for me, hobbies here happened almost by accident. I'd walk past a small gallery and stop in. I'd end up at a jazz set in a basement because a friend dragged me along. I started paying attention to photography again, partly because the city itself is so visually dense that you can't help wanting to capture it. And none of these started as a plan. That's what I value most. The barrier to trying something is so low, and the quality of what you encounter is so high, that curiosity gets rewarded very quickly.

I also think it feeds back into the research in a subtle way. A lot of what I do is about visual representation, about how machines see and understand the world. Spending time with people who think about images from a completely different angle, artists, photographers, filmmakers, actually changes the questions I ask. It reminds me that vision isn't just a benchmark. It's something humans care about deeply, for reasons that have nothing to do with accuracy numbers.

And honestly, it's good for your mental health. Research is a long game with a lot of failure. Having something outside of it that you're bad at and enjoy anyway keeps you grounded. New York makes that very easy to find.

r001.rationale: The guest values easily trying hobbies and describes actually visiting galleries, attending jazz, and pursuing photography. They do not say that simply having those opportunities brings joy even without using them.

You can take a class, go to an event, or meet someone who introduces you to a completely new hobby. You don’t have to decide in advance that this is going to become part of your identity—you can just explore. I really appreciate having that room to discover interests outside of work.

r001.rationale: The response appreciates the room to explore and the ease of trying new hobbies, but does not say that simply having those opportunities brings joy even without using them.

sol-6.1.text: What I value is the chance to step outside my usual routine. In New York, you can stumble into something you weren’t even looking for—a class, a performance, a whole community built around an interest you’ve never tried. You don’t have to commit to making it your next big thing. You can just be curious and be a beginner. I think having that space to explore is really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says the chance to explore is valuable and that one need not commit, but it does not clearly convey joy from the opportunities simply existing without taking advantage of them.
